Abstract

Manual penetration testing is characterized by high variance in methodology, tooling, and documentation, and it does not scale with the growth of modern attack surfaces. This monograph presents AstraIX Security Analyst, an AI-native, autonomous vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) platform that institutionalizes the assessment lifecycle as a deterministic, auditable, eight-stage pipeline. The platform orchestrates real security tooling — nmap, nikto, sqlmap, nuclei, gobuster, sslscan, and OWASP ZAP — inside isolated, disposable Kali Linux containers; normalizes heterogeneous tool output into a canonical finding model; enriches findings through an agentic pipeline comprising an orchestrated reconnaissance phase, a researcher agent grounded in a 360+ source cybersecurity knowledge base, and a verifier agent that re-exploits findings to suppress false positives; and closes the loop with deterministic risk scoring and AI-generated executive reporting.

Beyond functional design, the monograph reports a systematic evaluation of the codebase using automated code-intelligence tooling: a corpus of 4,038 files was structurally and semantically analyzed into an interactive knowledge graph of 4,669 nodes and 4,307 typed relationships, organized into ten architectural layers and a twelve-step guided tour. This evaluation verifies architectural coherence, quantifies layer distribution, and exposes the dependency structure of the system.

The monograph concludes with a security posture analysis, an operational model for container-isolated knowledge storage, and a staged research and product roadmap.

Keywords: autonomous security testing; vulnerability assessment; penetration testing; multi-agent systems; knowledge engineering; container orchestration; AI security

Chapter 1Introduction

1.1  Background and Motivation

Organizations today defend attack surfaces that grow continuously — new services, APIs, cloud tenants, third-party integrations, and AI-facing components appear faster than security teams can assess them. Against this backdrop, the vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) discipline remains disproportionately manual. A typical engagement requires a skilled operator to select tools, interpret heterogeneous tool output, manually correlate results across scanners, research remediation context, and author client-ready reporting. The outcome is expensive, slow, and — critically — variance-bound: two testers assessing the same target may produce materially different findings, severities, and documentation quality.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems have created a new design space: automating not merely the mechanical stages of assessment (launching tools, parsing output) but also the cognitive stages (contextual enrichment, validation, narrative synthesis). Simultaneously, containerization has matured to the point where real offensive tooling can be executed safely, reproducibly, and in isolation. AstraIX Security Analyst is a design and engineering artifact that occupies this design space.

1.2  Problem Statement

Problem Statement

Design and implement a platform that (i) executes real security tooling in an isolated, disposable execution environment; (ii) normalizes heterogeneous tool output into a single canonical finding model; (iii) applies AI to enrich and verify findings, reducing false positives; (iv) scores findings under a deterministic, defensible risk methodology; and (v) produces consistent executive deliverables — while remaining operationally deployable as a single containerized stack and instrumented for organizational multi-tenancy.

1.3  Design Questions

The work is organized around four design questions:

  1. DQ1 — Fidelity. How can a platform retain the fidelity of real tooling (as opposed to simulation) while guaranteeing isolation and reproducibility?
  2. DQ2 — Trust. How can AI augmentation improve rather than degrade the trustworthiness of findings — specifically, how can false positives be actively eliminated rather than merely flagged?
  3. DQ3 — Memory. How can institutional security knowledge be embedded in the platform such that enrichment is grounded, current, and operationally safe (including on host machines with aggressive antivirus)?
  4. DQ4 — Governance. How can risk methodology and reporting be made deterministic and consistent across engagements, testers, and organizations?

1.4  Contributions

The principal contributions of this work are:

  1. C1 — An autonomous assessment architecture. A container-orchestrated VAPT engine that executes real tooling (nmap, nikto, sqlmap, nuclei, gobuster, sslscan, OWASP ZAP) inside disposable Kali Linux containers, with a canonical SecurityFinding normalization layer.
  2. C2 — An agentic verification pipeline. A three-agent pipeline — orchestrated reconnaissance, knowledge-grounded enrichment, and re-exploitation-based verification — that operationalizes false-positive suppression.
  3. C3 — A container-isolated knowledge engineering subsystem. A 360+ source cybersecurity knowledge base with hybrid TF-IDF/FAISS retrieval, built-time ingestion, runtime extension, and host-filesystem immunity.
  4. C4 — A structured evaluation artifact. A codebase intelligence analysis of the full 4,038-file corpus, producing a 4,669-node knowledge graph with ten architectural layers and a guided tour — itself a reusable onboarding instrument.

1.5  Scope and Delimitations

This monograph covers the platform's design, architecture, pipeline, knowledge subsystem, evaluation, and operations. It does not claim empirical measurement of detection efficacy against benchmark corpora; systematic vulnerability-detection benchmarking is identified as future work (Section 9.2). All quantitative statements about the codebase (Chapter 6) were obtained by automated structural and semantic analysis of the repository at commit 8bd4966.

1.6  Document Structure

Chapter 2 situates the work in the assessment methodology and AI-security literature. Chapter 3 presents the system design and architecture. Chapter 4 specifies the autonomous assessment pipeline and its formal model. Chapter 5 details the knowledge engineering subsystem. Chapter 6 reports the codebase intelligence evaluation. Chapter 7 addresses deployment and operations; Chapter 8 treats security, ethics, and responsible use; Chapter 9 presents the roadmap; Chapter 10 concludes. Appendices collect configuration, API, statistics, and terminology.

Chapter 2Context and Related Work

2.1  Manual Assessment Methodology

Professional assessment practice is codified in several frameworks. The Penetration Testing Execution Standard (PTES) organizes engagements into pre-engagement interactions, intelligence gathering, threat modeling, vulnerability analysis, exploitation, post-exploitation, and reporting. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) maintains the Top 10 risk taxonomy and the Web Security Testing Guide, while NIST SP 800-115 frames technical security testing in the context of organizational security programs. AstraIX's eight-stage pipeline (Chapter 4) is a direct operationalization of this body of practice: targeting and scoping (pre-engagement), orchestrated reconnaissance (intelligence gathering), normalization and verification (vulnerability analysis and exploitation), and executive reporting (reporting).

2.2  Risk and Scoring Frameworks

Severity communication is dominated by the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), which yields base scores from exploitability and impact metrics. CVSS is effective for standardized disclosure but is less suited to engagement-level triage, where exploitability evidence, asset criticality, and verification state vary per finding. AstraIX therefore computes a deterministic engagement-level score in [0, 100] that composes technical severity, exploitability, asset criticality, and verification outcome (Section 4.5), while retaining CVSS-style terminology for stakeholder familiarity.

2.3  AI-Assisted and Agentic Security Platforms

A growing family of projects applies LLM agents to security assessment: PentAGI, Xalgorix, and Dark-Moon are representative open research platforms that drive offensive tooling through agentic planning loops. Their contributions establish the viability of LLM-driven scan planning and autonomous tool invocation. AstraIX differs in three respects: (i) it integrates with such platforms as interchangeable execution backends through an adapter layer, rather than binding to a single agent framework; (ii) it treats verification as a first-class stage with re-exploitation semantics rather than as a post-hoc annotation; and (iii) it grounds agent reasoning in an internally curated knowledge base rather than relying on the model's parametric memory alone.

Chapter 3System Design and Architecture

3.1  Design Principles

Six principles govern the architecture:

  1. Fidelity over simulation. Assessment quality depends on executing the actual toolchain; simulated results are an explicit opt-in demo mode, never the default.
  2. Determinism where possible, agency where necessary. Structural stages (execution, normalization, scoring) are deterministic; only enrichment and narrative stages are model-driven.
  3. Isolation by construction. All offensive execution occurs inside short-lived containers; the host never runs scanning tooling and never stores offensive payloads.
  4. Grounding over parametric memory. AI stages draw on a curated, versioned knowledge base through explicit retrieval.
  5. Extension by plugin. Tools and capabilities are first-class plugins with a canonical finding contract.
  6. Single-stack operability. The entire platform deploys as one Docker Compose topology.

3.2  Architectural Overview

Figure 3.1 shows the architecture. Three execution planes are distinguishable: the presentation plane (Next.js frontend behind nginx), the control plane (FastAPI backend and AI Security Core), and the execution plane (Kali containers, ZAP, and the knowledge base). Data flows from the presentation plane into the control plane via REST, and from the control plane into the execution plane through the Docker socket, with the knowledge base serving both the retrieval API and the agentic stages.

The attack-surface graph is a distinguishing feature: findings are not merely rows in a table but typed nodes related to assets, ports, and services, enabling relationship queries such as "all findings reachable from asset X" that are awkward in a relational model.

3.5  Platform Security Architecture

The platform's own security is treated as a first-class architectural concern: JWT-based authentication with refresh semantics; organization-scoped tenancy with role-based memberships and API-key access; the Docker socket as the sole host interface of the execution plane; container root execution constrained to disposable, network-isolated tool containers; and HTTP-only, path-traversal-safe knowledge access. Section 8.1 develops this posture in detail.

Chapter 4The Autonomous Assessment Pipeline

4.1  Formal Pipeline Model

Let T denote a target, A the set of enabled tool plugins, and Ot the raw output stream produced for tool t ∈ A. The pipeline is a composition of eight functions:

F = φverify ∘ φenrich ∘ φnorm ∘ φrecon(T, A)(4.1)

where φrecon produces a candidate finding set from tool output, φnorm maps heterogeneous output into the canonical model, φenrich augments each finding with knowledge-base evidence, and φverify re-executes targeted probes to confirm or refute each finding, yielding the verified set F. Scores are then assigned by the risk function ρ (Section 4.5), and narrative artifacts are generated by the reporting stage (Section 4.6). Determinism of φrecon…φverify is a design invariant; only enrichment and narrative stages are model-driven.

4.2  Stage Specification

Table 4.1 — Pipeline stage specification.
#StageInput → OutputDeterminism
1TargetingProject scope → target definition TDeterministic
2Orchestrated ReconT → tool output streams Ot (three phases, parallel)Deterministic
3NormalizationOt → canonical candidate findingsDeterministic
4Enrichmentcandidate findings → evidence-augmented findingsModel-driven
5Verificationaugmented findings → verified set FDeterministic (re-execution)
6Risk ScoringF → scores ρ(f) ∈ [0, 100]Deterministic
7Reportingscored findings → executive narrativeModel-driven
8Persistenceverified findings → relational + graph storesDeterministic

4.3  Multi-Agent Subsystem

Three cooperating agents implement the cognitive stages:

  1. ReconOrchestrator. Decomposes the assessment into three phases — recon, web, deep — and schedules tool plugins across them with parallel execution, maximizing coverage within declared scope.
  2. ResearcherAgent. For each candidate finding, retrieves relevant knowledge-base evidence (CVEs, remediation guidance, attack context) and appends it to the finding record. Retrieval is grounded in the curated corpus, not the model's parametric memory.
  3. VerifierAgent. Selects targeted re-execution probes for each finding; findings that cannot be re-confirmed are downgraded in severity or suppressed. This agent operationalizes the platform's core trust property: false positives do not reach stakeholders.

A planner component selects tooling and sequencing, and the system exposes a configurable execution backend through an adapter layer (Kali direct execution, and PentAGI / Xalgorix / Dark-Moon platform integrations), so the agentic substrate is swappable without disturbing the canonical finding contract.

4.4  Tool Execution and Normalization

Table 4.2 — Tool coverage of the execution plane.
ToolPurposePhase
nmapPort scanning, service detection, OS fingerprintingrecon
nucleiTemplate-based fast vulnerability scanningrecon / web
niktoWeb server vulnerability scanningweb
sqlmapSQL injection detection and exploitationweb
gobusterDirectory and DNS brute-forcingweb
sslscanSSL/TLS cipher and certificate analysisweb
OWASP ZAPAutomated web application security testingweb / deep

Execution follows a container-per-scan model: the executor accepts the tool specification and target, resolves the custom astraix-kali:latest image, spawns a disposable container through the Docker socket, streams output, and destroys the container on completion. The normalizer maps each tool's output grammar into the canonical SecurityFinding schema, which is the sole contract between the execution plane and the rest of the platform — the property that makes tool substitution and plugin extension safe.

4.5  Risk Scoring Model

The risk engine assigns each verified finding a score in [0, 100] as a weighted composition of four factors:

ρ(f) = wS·S(f) + wE·E(f) + wC·C(f) + wV·V(f)(4.2)

with S the technical severity factor (CVSS-aligned terminology), E the exploitability factor (evidence strength and ease), C the asset criticality factor (organization-contextual), and V the verification-state factor reflecting the verifier's confirmation result; weights are configuration-level constants, keeping the methodology deterministic and auditable across engagements. Scores feed the triage dashboard, the attack-surface graph, and executive reports unchanged, so stakeholders receive one consistent risk language.

4.6  AI Gateway and Reporting

The AI gateway is a model-agnostic interface to Gemini, used by the enrichment and narrative stages. The report engine renders standardized deliverables from verified, scored findings, so every engagement terminates in a consistent, client-ready artifact rather than raw scanner exports. Both stages are wrapped so that a model outage degrades quality (empty enrichment, templated narrative) without blocking the deterministic core.

Chapter 5Knowledge Engineering and AI Foundation

5.1  Corpus Construction

The knowledge base aggregates 360+ curated upstream sources — CVE repositories, exploitation references, methodology guides, and platform documentation — into a versioned corpus. Ingestion is build-time: a manifest (kb-repos.txt) drives cloning of upstream repositories inside the container build (fetch-kb), so sources never touch the host filesystem. This design was motivated by an operational constraint observed in practice: host antivirus products quarantine offensive-payload files, breaking host-side storage entirely. The corpus is seeded into a named volume (kb-data) at first boot and extended at runtime with kb-pull, which clones new sources directly into the container volume.

5.2  Retrieval Architecture

Retrieval is hybrid: TF-IDF lexical matching provides exact-term recall, while FAISS dense embeddings (≈109 MB index) provide semantic recall. Documents are chunked and embedded at seed time; the retrieval layer exposes ranked results to the researcher agent and to the HTTP API. Hybrid retrieval is a deliberate hedge — lexical grounding for precision on CVE identifiers and tool names, dense retrieval for paraphrase-level queries.

5.3  Knowledge Access APIs

Table 5.1 — Knowledge access API surface (verified).
Endpoint (group)Function

5.4  Training Data Infrastructure

Alongside the knowledge base, the platform ships curated training corpora: an SFT dataset of security knowledge instructions and a code-review SFT dataset of vulnerable-code analysis examples, plus community vulnerability datasets. These assets position the platform for fine-tuning of domain-adapted models — and, notably, for in-house evaluation of model safety and capability, consistent with an AI-security product mandate.

5.5  LLM Red-Teaming Capability

The platform extends its tooling into the AI domain: a PromptFoo-based LLM red-teaming capability (OWASP LLM Top 10-aligned plugins, grader-key passthrough, and direct-probe fallback) was integrated into the execution plane. This makes the platform's own AI stack — and client AI surfaces — first-class assessment targets, closing the loop between "AI-native" and "AI-tested."

Chapter 6Evaluation: Codebase Intelligence Analysis

6.1  Methodology

The repository was analyzed with Understand-Anything, a code-intelligence pipeline combining tree-sitter structural extraction with semantic analysis. The analysis pipeline executed in seven phases: scan (file inventory, language detection, import resolution), batch construction, per-batch semantic analysis, graph assembly and normalization, review, layer assignment, and guided-tour construction. All artifacts are reproducible from the repository (.ua/ data directory).

Table 6.4 — Edge type distribution.
Edge typeCountSemantics

Three structural observations follow. First, the module decomposition (675 contains, 613 exports, 553 imports) is balanced — the executable surface exhibits healthy modularity rather than monolith coupling. Second, the dependency structure is hierarchical: imports flow from API layer into services into domain, with the AI Security Core as a sink rather than a hub, indicating low cyclic coupling. Third, the 687 orphaned nodes are overwhelmingly corpus documents (475) and standalone configs (188), which is expected in a knowledge-heavy repository and does not indicate structural debt in the executable surface.

6.5  Threats to Validity

  1. Construct validity. Layer assignment and edge semantics rely on the analysis pipeline's conventions; mitigation was two-fold — validation scripts enforced one-layer-per-node coverage, and an independent review pass audited a sample of batches.
  2. Internal validity. Semantic summaries were generated by an LLM over structural extractions; they may overstate or miss functional detail. Grounding in tree-sitter structure bounds this risk.
  3. External validity. Findings characterize a single revision (8bd4966); the architecture is evolving by design (Chapter 9).

Chapter 7Deployment and Operations

7.1  Container Topology

Table 7.1 — Docker Compose service topology (verified).
ServiceImage / Role
postgresPostgreSQL 16 — primary datastore
redisRedis 7 — cache and coordination
neo4jNeo4j 5 — attack-surface graph
zapOWASP ZAP (stable) — web assessment engine
backendFastAPI application; bakes the knowledge base; Docker socket mounted
frontendNext.js application
nginxReverse proxy / ingress

7.2  Knowledge Base Lifecycle

The knowledge base follows a three-phase lifecycle: build (manifest-driven cloning into the image, via fetch-kb), seed (first-boot population of the kb-data volume via entrypoint.sh, gated on the absence of the chunk index), and extend (runtime ingestion via kb-pull, cloning directly into the container volume). Resetting the volume forces a full reseed from the image. This lifecycle enforces the host-immunity property end-to-end: no KB byte ever persists on the host.

7.3  Configuration and Secrets Management

Configuration is environment-driven; secrets exist only in the gitignored .env, while the tracked template (.env.example) carries placeholders. Key variables (Appendix A) include the Docker-execution switch, the demo-mode switch, the Kali image reference, and the database URL. Git credentials are managed via the OS keychain, and repository push-protection guards against accidental secret disclosure.

7.4  Observability

The backend exposes a health endpoint (/health) consumed by the compose healthcheck and by operators; per-stage pipeline progress is surfaced to the UI, and tool-level status is queryable through the VAPT tool health API. Structured observability (metrics, tracing) is identified as roadmap work.

Chapter 8Security, Ethics, and Responsible Use

8.1  Security Posture

Execution Isolation

All offensive tooling executes inside short-lived, disposable containers. The backend's only host interface to the execution plane is the Docker socket; containers are created per scan and destroyed on completion. No scanning tooling ever executes on the host process table.

Knowledge Integrity

Offensive payload sources never reside on the host filesystem. Corpus ingestion is build-internal and volume-bound; application access is HTTP-only through a path-traversal-safe retrieval API. This design also confers immunity to host AV quarantine events that would otherwise corrupt the corpus.

Identity and Tenancy

JWT authentication with refresh semantics; organization-scoped projects and findings; role-based memberships; API-key access for programmatic consumers.

Secrets Hygiene

Secrets confined to the gitignored environment file; repository push-protection; keychain-backed git credentials.

8.2  Ethical and Legal Considerations

Responsible Use

AstraIX is intended exclusively for authorized security assessments. Users are responsible for obtaining explicit, documented authorization before assessing any system. Unauthorized scanning may violate applicable law and licensing terms; the platform is distributed with this condition and no warranty.

9.2  Open Research Directions

  1. Detection-efficacy benchmarking. Systematic measurement against benchmark corpora (e.g., deliberately vulnerable applications) to quantify false-positive suppression attributable to the verifier stage.
  2. Verifier economics. Cost-latency trade-offs of re-exploitation; scheduling policies that bound re-execution to high-value findings.
  3. Retrieval quality. Ablation of lexical vs. dense retrieval across security-domain queries; construction of a domain-specific retrieval benchmark.
  4. Multi-tenant scaling. Isolation and fairness under concurrent organizational workloads; queueing semantics of the execution plane.
  5. LLM-as-target assessment. Maturation of the PromptFoo-based red-teaming capability into a formal LLM Top 10 assessment methodology.

Chapter 10Conclusion

This monograph presented AstraIX Security Analyst, an AI-native autonomous VAPT platform. The work demonstrates that the assessment lifecycle can be institutionalized as a deterministic, auditable pipeline in which real tooling executes in isolated containers, AI augments but never substitutes for verification, and knowledge — both institutional and operational — is engineered into the platform itself. The evaluation chapter established, through codebase-intelligence analysis of 4,038 files, that the executable surface is modular and hierarchical, that the knowledge layer dominates the corpus by design, and that the entire system is navigable through a structured, layered knowledge graph.

The platform's deepest design commitments — fidelity, verification, grounding, isolation, and determinism — align it with the emerging standard for trustworthy AI-assisted security operations. The roadmap commits to measurement, scale, and the maturation of LLM-facing assessment, keeping AstraIX at the frontier of the discipline it automates.

  10. Dark-Moon. Autonomous AI pentest platform. Available: https://darkmoon.ai/

  12. Understand-Anything. Multi-platform agentic code knowledge-graph tool. Available: https://github.com/Egonex-AI/Understand-Anything
  13. AstraIX Security Analyst. Product repository. Available: https://github.com/pentestparas/ASTRAIX--AI-Autonomous-Security-Platform

Appendix AConfiguration Variables

Table A.1 — Principal configuration variables.
VariableDefaultDescription
VAPT_USE_DOCKERtrueEnables real Docker-based VAPT execution
VAPT_DEMO_MODEfalseSimulated, tool-less results (explicit opt-in)
KALI_IMAGEastraix-kali:latestExecution image for tool containers
DATABASE_URLpostgresql+asyncpg://…PostgreSQL connection string
SECRET_KEYrequiredJWT signing key
KB_SYNC_REPOSfalseRuntime re-synchronization of manifest sources

Appendix DGlossary of Terms

TermDefinition
VAPTVulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing
Canonical findingThe normalized SecurityFinding model shared by all tools and plugins
Recon phaseParallel discovery stage (recon / web / deep) executed by the ReconOrchestrator
Verifier agentAgent that re-executes targeted probes to confirm or downgrade findings
kb-pullRuntime ingestion command that clones KB sources into the container volume
Attack-surface graphNeo4j-persisted network of assets, findings, and relationships
Codebase intelligenceAutomated structural + semantic analysis of a repository into a queryable graph
